title: Cloudflare service token overwrite causes 121-minute outage
rawText:
Impact
WARP and Zero Trust users were unable to enroll new devices or upgrade app versions. Cache Purge, Cache Reserve, Images, and R2 services had elevated failure rates. Gateway device posture rules defaulted to blocking traffic, peaking at over 50,000 5XX errors per minute. Approximately 10.5 million posture read errors were recorded. The outage lasted 121 minutes from first impact at 17:50 UTC to full resolution at 19:51 UTC on January 24 2023.

Timeline
16:55 UTC - Code release initiated containing service token metadata changes.
17:05 UTC - Release rolled back after errors detected; token overwrites had already occurred.
17:50 UTC - First invalid WARP token synced to edge; customer impact begins.
18:12 UTC - Incident formally declared by on-call engineer.
18:19 UTC - First invalid API token synced; Cache services begin experiencing elevated errors.
18:21 UTC - Root cause identified by engineering team.
18:51 UTC - WARP account token restored from backup; WARP impact ends.
18:56 UTC - API account token restored.
19:00 UTC - Accidental re-overwrite of API account token occurred.
19:07 UTC - Correct API token value restored again.
19:51 UTC - All four affected accounts fully restored from backup; incident closes.

Root Cause
A code release added a 'Last seen at' timestamp field to service tokens using a read-modify-write pattern. The read step returned redacted (empty string) secrets for security reasons. The write step then persisted these empty strings over the original client_secret values. This silently corrupted the credentials of four internal Cloudflare service accounts that power WARP, Zero Trust, Cache, and Images services. The bug was not caught by existing unit tests because tests did not assert that token secrets remained unchanged after metadata updates.

Fix
Engineers restored the four affected service accounts from database backups. Unit tests were added to catch any future token overwrite regressions. Automatic alerting was implemented for dramatic increases in failed authentication requests. Empty string validation was added to the service token database fields alongside existing null checks. Faster database rollback procedures were documented and implemented.

title: GitHub DNS outage from Puppet manifest bug causes 42 minutes of downtime
rawText:
Impact
GitHub experienced 42 minutes of complete service downtime starting at approximately 13:30 PST on January 8 2014. After partial restoration, an additional 1 hour and 35 minutes of partial downtime affected a subset of repositories due to zone file corruption and fileserver memory exhaustion. Error rates were significantly elevated throughout the recovery period. All GitHub.com users were unable to access repositories during the full outage window.

Timeline
13:20 PST - Rollout of DNS firewall and router configuration changes begins.
13:29 PST - Changes deployed to second authoritative name server.
13:30 PST - DNS query timeouts begin manifesting for external users.
13:49 PST - Caching and authoritative name servers reloaded; initial timeouts resolved.
13:50 PST - NXDOMAIN errors appear; zone file corruption discovered by engineers.
14:30 PST - Fileserver memory exhaustion and process proliferation identified as secondary problem.
15:47 PST - Full service restoration completed.

Root Cause
A Puppet manifest bug caused only the authoritative name server to be restarted during the configuration deployment. The caching name server was not restarted. This created a circular dependency: the DNS deployment triggered internal API calls that required functioning DNS to complete, but DNS was partially broken. Because API responses were not validated before being written to the zone file, a corrupted zone file was produced. Separately, fileservers spawned excessive processes during the outage, exhausting available memory and creating routing layer back pressure that prolonged recovery.

Fix
Internal and external DNS infrastructure were decoupled to allow independent changes without circular dependencies. Configuration management code was reviewed and improved with rspec-puppet testing. API response validation was added before any zone file updates. Safety mechanisms in the fileserver management and routing layers were tested and repaired. Linux cgroups were implemented to limit application process resource consumption. Tight DNS dependencies in fileserver code were eliminated.

title: Facebook global outage from BGP backbone misconfiguration takes down all properties
rawText:
Impact
All Meta platforms including Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and internal tools were completely unavailable globally for approximately six hours on October 4 2021. The outage disconnected all Facebook data centers globally. Internal tools and communication systems that relied on the same infrastructure were also inaccessible, making remote incident response difficult. Billions of users worldwide were unable to access any Meta service.

Timeline
The outage began when a routine maintenance command was issued to assess backbone network capacity. The command inadvertently disabled all global backbone connections simultaneously. Facebook's DNS servers, which relied on the backbone, withdrew their BGP route advertisements and became unreachable from the internet. Facebook domains effectively disappeared from the global DNS. Engineers attempted remote resolution but were unable to access internal systems due to the same infrastructure outage. Physical access to data centers was required but delayed by security protocols. Engineers were physically deployed to data centers. Systems were manually restarted to restore backbone connectivity. Services were brought back gradually using storm drill protocols to prevent cascading failures from the sudden traffic surge. Full service restoration completed several hours after the outage began.

Root Cause
A maintenance engineer issued a command intended to assess backbone network capacity. The command unintentionally disabled all connections in the global backbone network. An audit tool designed to prevent such errors contained a bug that failed to block the erroneous command. With the backbone offline, BGP route advertisements for Facebook's DNS servers were withdrawn, making the infrastructure unreachable. The security safeguards at data centers slowed physical access needed for manual recovery.

Fix
Engineers physically accessed data centers and performed manual system restarts to restore backbone connectivity. Gradual service restoration using storm drill protocols managed the traffic surge to prevent secondary failures. Meta reviewed and fixed the audit tool bug that failed to block the dangerous command. Access and recovery procedures were improved so physical intervention during a network-level outage could happen faster.

title: GoCardless API outage from Pacemaker misconfiguration prevents automated database failover
rawText:
Impact
All GoCardless API requests failed for 1 hour and 50 minutes on October 10 2017 from 15:09 to 16:59 UTC. The API and Dashboard were completely unavailable during this window. Payment processing was interrupted for all merchants using the GoCardless platform. The outage would normally have been a 1 to 2 minute automated failover event but became a 110-minute manual recovery due to cluster configuration errors.

Timeline
15:09 UTC - Outage detected; disk array failure identified on the primary database node.
15:17 UTC - Primary node powered off manually after disk failure confirmed.
15:17 UTC - Pacemaker cluster fails to automatically promote replica due to misconfiguration.
16:18 UTC - Manual promotion of synchronous replica attempted by on-call engineers.
16:59 UTC - Services restored; monitoring confirmed API and Dashboard back online.

Root Cause
A hardware disk array failure on the primary PostgreSQL database triggered what should have been an automated failover. Three simultaneous Pacemaker configuration errors prevented the automatic failover: the default-resource-stickiness setting kept resources pinned to the failed primary, the backup VIP had a negative infinity colocation constraint preventing it from moving, and a simultaneous process crash on the synchronous replica confused the cluster state machine. The combination of these three conditions caused Pacemaker to fail silently rather than promote the replica.

Fix
Pacemaker colocation rules were corrected by reversing the negative infinity colocation constraint to a positive infinity preference. The database cluster was migrated to a new cluster with fully audited configuration. VIP-based routing was replaced with application-level proxy management to eliminate single points of failure. Enhanced fault injection testing was implemented to regularly validate cluster failover behavior under realistic failure scenarios.

title: CircleCI jobs stuck not running due to backwards-incompatible database schema change
rawText:
Impact
All CircleCI jobs were blocked in a non-running state across all executors from 18:50 to 19:43 UTC on November 8 2021, a period of approximately 53 minutes. Extended queue delays persisted until 20:19 UTC as the backlog of stuck jobs was processed. The incident affected all CI/CD pipelines running on CircleCI during the window.

Timeline
18:50 UTC - Database field type change deployed to production.
18:50 UTC - Errors immediately detected in job distribution service.
18:52 UTC - Rollback of the deployment initiated.
18:52 UTC - Post-rollback, data written during the brief deploy window became unreadable.
18:55 UTC - Job distribution continues to fail due to unreadable data records.
19:05 UTC - Manual fix deployed to allow distribution system to ignore the problematic field.
19:15 UTC - Compute cluster manually scaled to process backlog.
19:43 UTC - Job flow fully resumed.
20:19 UTC - Normal processing confirmed with queue drained.

Root Cause
A deployment changed a PostgreSQL field type in a non-backwards-compatible way in the job distribution service. The schema migration was not tested against the production data volume or schema validation rules. When the deployment was rolled back, data records written during the brief deployment window contained values in the new field type that could not be read by the old schema, causing the distribution service to fail continuously on those records.

Fix
Engineers deployed a code modification that instructed the distribution system to skip and ignore records with the problematic unreadable field values. The compute cluster was manually scaled to accelerate processing of the stuck job backlog. The team implemented additional pre-deployment database schema validation checks. Backwards-compatibility testing was added to the deployment pipeline to catch field type changes before they reach production.

title: GitLab accidental production database deletion causes 18-hour outage and 6 hours of data loss
rawText:
Impact
GitLab.com was unavailable for approximately 18 hours beginning January 31 2017 after accidental deletion of the primary PostgreSQL database. Approximately 300 GB of data was deleted. Modifications to projects, comments, user accounts, issues, and snippets between 17:20 UTC January 31 and midnight were permanently lost. Roughly 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments, and 700 new user accounts were destroyed and could not be recovered. The data loss window was 6 hours. The incident became public knowledge in real time as GitLab engineers streamed recovery efforts live.

Timeline
17:20 UTC Jan 31 - Spam-related database load spike begins causing replication lag on secondary.
19:00 UTC - An engineer attempts to resync the lagging secondary database.
19:00 UTC - Engineer accidentally executes database directory wipe command against the primary server instead of the secondary.
19:02 UTC - Engineer notices the mistake and terminates the process; 300 GB already deleted.
19:05 UTC - Engineers begin searching for database backups.
19:30 UTC - Automated pg_dump backups discovered to have never run due to misconfiguration.
20:00 UTC - LVM snapshots found to be 0 bytes and unusable.
20:30 UTC - Azure disk snapshots found to be taken before the data loss window.
21:00 UTC - A manual snapshot taken 6 hours before data loss by an engineer doing a test is identified as the only viable restore point.
Feb 1 09:00 UTC - Limited GitLab.com service restored after approximately 18 hours of work.

Root Cause
An engineer intended to wipe the PostgreSQL data directory on the secondary replica to resync it with the primary. Due to terminal session confusion during a stressful incident, the wipe command was executed on the primary production server instead of the secondary. The catastrophic impact was compounded by multiple independent backup system failures: automated pg_dump backups had never run due to a silent misconfiguration where backup failure alerts were sent to an email address that was silently rejecting messages due to DMARC policy. The pg_dump restore procedure was also incompatible because the backup tooling used PostgreSQL 9.2 while production ran PostgreSQL 9.6. LVM snapshots existed but were 0 bytes due to a separate misconfiguration. No engineer had been assigned ownership or responsibility for validating the backup system.

Fix
GitLab restored from the 6-hour-old manual snapshot taken by an engineer for testing purposes, which was the only viable backup. Automated full database restoration into a staging environment was implemented and scheduled weekly to continuously validate that backups actually work. A dedicated engineer was assigned ownership of the backup system with authority to halt deployments if data safety was at risk. All backup failure alerting was audited and repaired. The pg_dump tooling version mismatch was corrected. A second person rule was proposed for any destructive database operations. GitLab published the full postmortem publicly including the live recovery stream.
